pages.blurb: The Lancashire warehouse raves of 1989–90, thousands every weekend.

pages.name: Ghent
pages.blurb: R&S Records and the hoover; Belgium's new beat around it.

pages.name: Ibiza
pages.blurb: Pacha, Amnesia, Ku, Space, DC10: open-air terraces roofed over by noise rules in the early 1990s (Space's excepted), and techno's summer residency since 2000.

pages.name: Manchester
pages.blurb: The Haçienda, Madchester, Bugged Out, 808 State and A Guy Called Gerald.

pages.name: Rotterdam
pages.blurb: Gabber: Parkzicht and Rotterdam Records; the Thunderdome raves, first held in Friesland in 1992, carried its sound across the country.

pages.name: ageHa
pages.blurb: Tokyo's largest nightclub for two decades, in Studio Coast on the Shin-Kiba waterfront, with a poolside terrace; closed on 30 January 2022.

pages.blurb: Naji Gebran's club, moved in 1998 to Bernard Khoury's sunken building at Karantina with a retracting circular roof.

pages.name: The Ballroom Blitz
pages.blurb: Three-room club in an old textile factory near Beirut's port, with a small Gold Room for experimental music.

pages.name: Big Beat Boutique
pages.blurb: Norman Cook and Damian Harris's Friday night at the Concorde, begun in 1995 or 1996, which by Cook's account gave big beat its name.

pages.name: Brixton Academy
pages.blurb: The all-nighters that put rave in a theatre.

pages.name: Cakeshop
pages.blurb: Itaewon basement opened in September 2012 by Gabriel Joseph and Samuel Swanson; Seoul's room for bass, grime, gqom and baile funk.

pages.name: Club 2019
pages.blurb: Junkyard club at Maslak run by Ceylan Çaplı and Mehmet Cavcı; its team launched the techno station Radio 2019.

pages.name: Crash, Vauxhall
pages.blurb: Wayne Shires's railway-arch club in Vauxhall, which he called his version of New York's Tunnel.

pages.name: Dalston Superstore
pages.blurb: Bar-club opened in May 2009 by Dan Beaumont and Matt Tucker; its basement grew Body Movements and Mighty Hoopla.

pages.name: Drugstore
pages.blurb: Techno club in a former Belgrade slaughterhouse, opened in 2012; it stayed closed on 24 January 2025 for the general strike in support of the student-led protests.

pages.name: The Eclipse
pages.blurb: Britain's first legal all-night rave club; Doc Scott's home.

pages.name: Fairfield Halls
pages.blurb: Park Lane concert hall opened on 2 November 1962; Kraftwerk and Tangerine Dream played it in autumn 1975.

pages.name: Fold
pages.blurb: Canning Town, 24-hour licence, no photos.

pages.name: The Garage (Nottingham)
pages.blurb: Selectadisc's Lace Market club, opened 1983: Graeme Park's first residency, where he moved from post-punk and electro to Chicago house by 1986.

pages.name: Golden Pudel
pages.blurb: A small, independent club on the Fischmarkt in St Pauli, Hamburg, which brought through Helena Hauff.

pages.name: Hard Wax
pages.blurb: Mark Ernestus's record shop; the city's centre of gravity.

pages.name: Hilltop
pages.blurb: Open-air palm-grove party ground behind Little Vagator: Sunday trance until 10pm, a festival since at least 2008, and still running in 2024.

pages.name: Ice Palace (Cherry Grove)
pages.blurb: Michael Fesco's foil-walled club in Cherry Grove, modelled on the Sanctuary, which replaced the jukebox with a DJ in 1970.

pages.name: Kablys
pages.blurb: Arts venue in Vilnius's 1956 railway workers' Palace of Culture, home to what Lithuanian Music Link calls the country's first raves, with a club from 2013.

pages.name: Komrads
pages.blurb: Club at 1 Isabella Street, near Yonge and Wellesley, with a steel dance floor; for a time Toronto's only permanent after-hours club.

pages.name: Lakota
pages.blurb: Bristol's jungle and drum & bass room; opened 1989 by Wikipedia's account, though the club dates itself from June 1992.

pages.name: Liquid Room
pages.blurb: Kabukichō then Ebisu; Mills, 28 October 1995.

pages.name: Midnight Shift
pages.blurb: Club at 85–91 Oxford Street, known for its Hellfire Club night; it announced its closure for 1 October 2017.

pages.name: The Music Institute
pages.blurb: Juice bar at 1315 Broadway, midnight to 9am, from May 1988 until it closed in November 1989.

pages.name: NYC Downlow
pages.blurb: Block9's temporary gay club at Glastonbury, first built in 2007 as a ruined New York tenement and co-produced with Horse Meat Disco.

pages.name: Output
pages.blurb: Williamsburg club on Wythe Avenue with a Funktion-One rig including prototypes; closed at the start of 2019, after John Digweed's set on 31 December 2018.

pages.name: Paradise Garage
pages.blurb: Larry Levan; the sound system and the congregation.

pages.name: Plastic
pages.blurb: Milan's queer and underground club, opened 23 December 1980 and closed in June 2025.

pages.name: Propaganda (Moscow)
pages.blurb: Moscow club where Nina Kraviz held a regular night from 2008.

pages.name: Renaissance
pages.blurb: Venue 44; Sasha and Digweed; the progressive house residency.

pages.name: The Sanctuary
pages.blurb: Helter Skelter and Dreamscape's arena; the home of hardcore.

pages.name: Shiva Valley
pages.blurb: Beach shack beside Curlies at the south end of Anjuna, known for its Tuesday sundown psytrance party; opening date undocumented.

pages.name: Spectrum
pages.blurb: Paul Oakenfold's Monday at Heaven from April 1988, and acid house's first big room.

pages.name: Sub Club
pages.blurb: Jamaica Street basement; Slam's Subculture since 1994.

pages.name: The Fridge
pages.blurb: Brixton: Love Muscle, Escape from Samsara (trance), the big rave nights.

pages.name: The Pig, Hastings
pages.blurb: The Hastings venue where Detroit Techno Militia played with the Hastings Techno Militia on 27 December 2024.

pages.name: The Trip
pages.blurb: Nicky Holloway at the Astoria; the crowd dancing in the Charing Cross Road fountain.

pages.name: Turnmills
pages.blurb: Clerkenwell: Trade on Sunday mornings (house strand), The Gallery, and most of London's techno guests in between.

pages.name: Ushuaïa Ibiza
pages.blurb: Palladium's open-air hotel club on Platja d'en Bossa, opened 2011: daytime shows from Guetta, Garrix and Avicii, and the seed of Hï Ibiza and UNVRS.

pages.name: Warsaw Ballroom
pages.blurb: South Beach gay club at Collins Avenue and Espanola Way, run from 1989 by Andrew Delaplaine.

pages.name: Xlib
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Basement club on Kyrylivska Street in Podil, among Kyiv's first unglamorous electronic rooms by LB.ua's account.

pages.name: Association of Independent Festivals
pages.blurb: British trade body for independent festivals; counts the festivals lost each year and ran the first full sector count in 2025.

pages.name: Bhavishyavani Future Soundz
pages.blurb: Mumbai collective whose founders included Ashim Ahluwalia, Mukul Deora and Tejas Mangeshkar; parties from 13 May 1999.

pages.name: Bronski Beat
pages.blurb: Jimmy Somerville, Steve Bronski and Larry Steinbachek, whose 1984 hit "Smalltown Boy" reached number three in Britain.

pages.name: Detroit Techno Militia
pages.blurb: Street-level Detroit DJ-and-producer collective "dedicated to preserving the legacy of true Detroit electronic music": T.Linder, DJ Seoul, Darkcube, Neil V, DJ Psycho, J.Garcia. Label launched 2007; the DTM 5x5 (five DJs, five turntables, 2007); Detroit Music Award 2010; the Made in Detroit stage at Movement 2011; The Grid radio show (2013). Since 2023 a regular guest in Hastings.

pages.name: Drug checking in Zürich (Streetwork and DIZ)
pages.blurb: The city's mobile drug checking from 2001 and fixed testing at the Drogeninformationszentrum from 2006; a stand at the Street Parade.

pages.name: Good Night Out Campaign
pages.blurb: Campaign begun by Hollaback London in March 2014 that trains and accredits venues to deal with sexual harassment.

pages.name: ID&T
pages.blurb: Dutch promoter of Thunderdome and Mysteryland, co-founded by Duncan Stutterheim; sold to SFX in 2013 and to Superstruct in 2021.

pages.name: Killasan
pages.blurb: Osaka reggae sound system crew; a quarter of its club system, shipped to Berlin about 2001, became the centre of the Wax Treatment parties.

pages.name: Major League DJz
pages.blurb: Twins Banele and Bandile Mbere, whose rooftop Balcony Mix streams spread amapiano in lockdown; sold out O2 Academy Brixton in 2022.

pages.name: Moroko Loko
pages.blurb: Amine K's underground party series, started in 2009 against the clubs' commercial music, later holding poolside parties in Marrakech.

pages.name: Papi Juice
pages.blurb: Party and art collective founded by Oscar Nñ and Adam Rhodes for queer and transgender people of colour; first night held in a 72-person bar.

pages.name: Quando Quango
pages.blurb: Factory Records dance group formed by Hillegonda Rietveld and Mike Pickering; "Love Tempo" (1983) was remixed in New York.

pages.name: Saffron
pages.blurb: Bristol label and training project founded by Laura Lewis-Paul, teaching production and DJing to women and gender non-conforming people.

pages.name: Adam Smith and Marcus Lyall
pages.blurb: Show directors of the Chemical Brothers since 2009; Smith has made the duo's visuals since their first gig in 1995.

pages.name: Superjane
pages.blurb: Chicago collective of DJ Heather, Colette, Lady D and Dayhota, who say they were America's first all-woman DJ group.

pages.name: Tuff Jam
pages.blurb: DJ and production duo Matt Jam Lamont and Karl Tuff Enuff Brown, Kiss presenters from 1997 to 2000 and central figures in underground garage.

pages.name: A Club Called Rhonda
pages.blurb: House and disco night begun by Loren Granic and Gregory Alexander, which grew from Guatelinda to Los Globos with a mixed, queer-friendly crowd.

pages.name: Afterlife
pages.blurb: Tale Of Us's melodic-techno party and label: Space in 2016, Privilege in 2017, then Thursdays at Hï Ibiza from 2018, built around big-screen visuals.

pages.name: A.R.T. at Yellow
pages.blurb: K.U.D.O.'s Friday at Yellow in Tokyo, renamed Zero from 1994.

pages.name: Atlas Electronic
pages.blurb: Karim Mrabti's festival at Villa Janna, capped at 2,000 a day, mixing club DJs with gnawa and desert bands.

pages.name: AWOL
pages.blurb: A Way of Life at the Paradise Club, jungle's home.

pages.name: Bass Culture
pages.blurb: D'Julz's monthly residency at the Rex Club from 1997, the longest-standing in the club's history; it marked twenty years in 2017 and played the old room's last party on 27 May 2023.

pages.name: Bestival
pages.blurb: Rob and Josie da Bank's festival on the Isle of Wight, then Lulworth; Bestival Ltd went into administration in October 2018.

pages.name: Biyoshi Night
pages.blurb: Yellow's Monday from 1994 to 1999, the hairdressers' night.

pages.name: Body & Soul (New York)
pages.blurb: Sunday-afternoon party at Vinyl run by François Kevorkian and John Davis, with Danny Krivit and Joe Claussell, for a mixed crowd.

pages.name: Brave! Factory
pages.blurb: Closer's festival at the disused Metrobud train repair works in western Kyiv, first held in late August 2017.

pages.name: Catchmydrift?
pages.blurb: The Hastings promoter who brought over Detroit Techno Militia (Easter Sunday 2023, December 2024, Easter Sunday 2026) and incubated the Hastings Techno Militia.

pages.name: Coachella's Sahara and Yuma tents
pages.blurb: Coachella's dance tents: the Sahara, as old as the festival and rebuilt for 2024, and the air-conditioned Yuma from 2013.

pages.name: Creamfields Buenos Aires
pages.blurb: Cream's Argentine festival, from San Isidro in 2001 to Puerto Madero and the Costanera Sur; back at Parque de la Ciudad in 2024, under Fénix Entertainment in 2025.

pages.name: Defqon.1
pages.blurb: Q-dance's hardstyle festival, at Almere from 2003 and Biddinghuizen from 2011; over 72,000 a day; cancelled for heat in 2026.

pages.name: Djakarta Warehouse Project
pages.blurb: Ismaya Live's festival, from Jakarta's clubs to the Jakarta International Expo and, by 2023, Bali.

pages.name: Dub War
pages.blurb: Dave Q and Joe Nice's night, the first dubstep night in the United States, begun in a Bed-Stuy basement.

pages.name: EDC Mexico
pages.blurb: Insomniac and OCESA's edition at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, Mexico City, from 2014; more than 250,000 in 2025 by Electronic Groove's count.

pages.name: Electric Zoo
pages.blurb: Made Event's Labor Day festival on Randall's Island; final day cancelled after two deaths in 2013; failed weekend in 2023.

pages.name: Festival Estéreo Picnic
pages.blurb: Páramo Presenta's Bogotá festival, from 2,800 in 2010 to 152,000 over four days in 2025.

pages.name: Fantazia: The Big Bang
pages.blurb: Ten-hour licensed rave at the SECC for about 12,000, documented cable by cable in Music Technology at a cost of upwards of £250,000.

pages.name: Forbidden Forest
pages.blurb: Dance festival at Belvoir Castle, licensed by Melton in 2022 after bass complaints; the Arcadia Spider played its tenth edition in 2026.

pages.name: Fuckparade
pages.blurb: Berlin's yearly counter-demonstration to the Love Parade, started as the Hateparade in 1997 for gabber and hardcore; a court confirmed it as a demo in 2007.

pages.name: Genesis
pages.blurb: Wayne Anthony's warehouse parties in East London; "Class of 88".

pages.name: Glastonbury Festival
pages.blurb: The festival at Worthy Farm, where dance music moved from market stalls and travellers' fields to the Pyramid Stage between 1989 and 1997.

pages.name: Happy Days
pages.blurb: Timi Ram Jam's Sunday afterparty for Ministry of Sound clubbers, which moved from a pub to the Frog & Nightgown and the Arches.

pages.name: Homelands
pages.blurb: Mean Fiddler's dance festival on the Matterley Bowl, drawing more than 50,000 at its height; the last was in May 2005.

pages.name: Houghton
pages.blurb: Craig Richards's 24-hour licence.

pages.name: Judgement Sundays
pages.blurb: Judge Jules's Sunday night at Eden in San Antonio, one of the Ibiza residencies of the trance years.

pages.name: Kazantip
pages.blurb: A weeks-long Crimean beach 'republic' founded by Nikita Marshunok; moved to Anaklia, Georgia, in 2014 after Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

pages.name: La Espuma
pages.blurb: Amnesia's weekly foam party under that name: Sundays in 2005 to pop, hip-hop and reggaeton, Saturdays shared with Foam & Diamonds by 2015, Wednesdays in the Club room by 2018.

pages.name: Isles of Wonder: the London 2012 opening ceremony
queries: "Isles of Wonder: the London 2012 opening ceremony" London nightclub
"Isles of Wonder: the London 2012 opening ceremony" London
pages.blurb: Danny Boyle's Olympic opening ceremony of 27 July 2012, its music directed by Underworld's Rick Smith.

pages.name: Love Parade
pages.blurb: 150 people on the Ku'damm on 1 July 1989; 1.5 million by 1999; Duisburg, 24 July 2010.

pages.name: Manumission
pages.blurb: The McKays' theatrical Monday at Ku, then Privilege: 8,000–10,000 people, stage shows and the Motel, from 1994 until it ended at Amnesia in 2008.

pages.name: Melt
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Festival held from 1999 among the mining excavators of Ferropolis; its organisers ended it after the July 2024 edition.

pages.name: Monegros Desert Festival
pages.blurb: The Arnau family's desert rave outside Fraga, cancelled in 2015 over a family land dispute and revived in 2022.

pages.name: Music On
pages.blurb: Marco Carola's long-set tech-house night: Fridays at Amnesia from 2012 to 2018, then at Pacha from 2019, where it still runs on Fridays.

pages.name: Neversea
pages.blurb: Untold's beach festival in Constanța from 2017; it did not run in 2025, its organisers said, for lack of a suitable beach sector.

pages.name: Nude
pages.blurb: Mike Pickering's Friday at the Haçienda, established by early 1986 with Little Martin Prendergast and later Graeme Park: salsa, electro and northern soul at first, then the first Chicago house records.

pages.name: Paradise
pages.blurb: Jamie Jones's Hot Creations party: eight seasons at DC10 from 2012, Wednesdays at Amnesia from 2022 and at UNVRS since 2025.

pages.name: Pervert
pages.blurb: Roving queer techno party begun in April 2017 by Alberto Herbel and Robin Garcia, with a dark room at every night.

pages.name: Queen! at Smartbar
pages.blurb: Sunday queer night at Smartbar founded by Michael Serafini and Garrett David, with drag hosts booked as carefully as DJs.

pages.name: Return to the Source
pages.blurb: The Fridge; Goa trance in Brixton.

pages.name: Sandbox Festival
pages.blurb: Red Sea festival at El Gouna, Egypt; about 5,000 visitors at its tenth anniversary in 2024, by Mixmag.

pages.name: Section 28
pages.blurb: Clause barring councils from promoting homosexuality, law from 24 May 1988 until repeal in Scotland (2000) and England and Wales (2003).

pages.name: Shambhala Music Festival
pages.blurb: Family-run, sponsor-free festival on the Salmo River Ranch in British Columbia, with crew-run stages and PK Sound rigs, by EDM Maniac's account in 2024.

pages.name: Snax
pages.blurb: Norbert Thormann and Michael Teufele's party, begun in 1994 in the Reichsbahnbunker on Albrechtstraße in Mitte; it led them to Ostgut in 1998 and Berghain in 2004, and still takes over Berghain at Easter.

pages.name: Speed Queen
pages.blurb: Leeds Saturday that started at the Warehouse, moved to Stinky's Peep House, where about 350 came to a terrace and a giant bed, and returned to the Warehouse in 2003 before Gatecrasher and Mint Warehouse.

pages.name: Subculture
pages.blurb: Slam's Saturday at the Sub Club since 9 April 1994, with Harri and Domenic as residents: the longest-running weekly in the UK.

pages.name: Sunrise
pages.blurb: Tony Colston-Hayter's parties: White Waltham airfield, Santa Pod raceway; "Sunrise 5000"; the Sun's front page.

pages.name: Telepathy
pages.blurb: East London's jungle rave.

pages.name: Time Warp
pages.blurb: 26 November 1994, Ludwigshafen, 2,000 people; the Maimarkthalle since 2000.

pages.name: Torba Party
pages.blurb: Vitalii Ulitskyi's party series: fifteen nights of house, jungle and video at Flamingo, New York and the House of Cinema.

pages.name: Tribe
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Brazilian psytrance festival founded by Du Serena with about 50 people; 25,000 by 2005, later at Parque Maeda in Itu.

pages.name: Ultra Music Festival
pages.blurb: Miami's March festival: Collins Park, Bayfront and Bicentennial Parks, Virginia Key in 2019, then Bayfront under a 55,000 daily cap.

pages.name: UNUM
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: A round-the-clock house, techno and minimal festival on Albania's north-west coast, first held in 2019.

pages.name: Whirl-Y-Gig
pages.blurb: All-ages world and dance club begun by Ros Madden in 1981 and run since the mid-1980s by DJ Monkey Pilot and Mary Sutcliffe.

pages.name: Wonderfruit
pages.blurb: Music and arts festival on the Fields at Siam Country Club, Chonburi, capped at about 25,000 a day by 2025.

pages.name: XXXperience
pages.blurb: Independent Brazilian trance festival begun by DJ Feio and Rica Amaral in 1996 for about 400 people.

pages.name: Agent of Change
pages.blurb: The planning principle that makes developers, not venues, responsible for soundproofing: from the 2017 housing white paper into the planning framework in 2018, with the Ministry of Sound's Eileen House settlement as an early precedent.

pages.name: Form 696
pages.blurb: The Met's risk-assessment form that asked promoters for the audience's ethnicity until 2008–09; blamed for closing grime and garage nights, scrapped in 2017.

pages.name: Misuse of Drugs Act 1971
pages.blurb: The Act that classifies MDMA as Class A; the framework every later policy argument has been held inside.

pages.name: Psychoactive Substances Act 2016
pages.blurb: The blanket ban on "legal highs" and nitrous oxide's long road to a 2023 ban.

pages.name: WHO Global Standard for Safe Listening Venues and Events
queries: "WHO Global Standard for Safe Listening Venues and Events"
pages.blurb: WHO's six features for venues: 100 dB average over 15 minutes, monitoring, acoustics, earplugs, quiet zones, trained staff.

pages.name: Akai S900 / S950
pages.blurb: Sampler — The first affordable rack sampler: S900s and S950s cut "Voodoo Ray" and much breakbeat hardcore after it; the S950 had the first, crude timestretch.

pages.name: AlphaTheta XDJ-AZ
pages.blurb: Four-deck all-in-one standalone DJ system, October 2024, £2,799, laid out after the CDJ-3000 and DJM-A9.

pages.name: Behringer clones
pages.blurb: Drum machine — The RD-8, TD-3 and Model D copy the 808, 303 and Minimoog exactly for less than a night out. The machines of 1982 became the machines of 2020.

pages.name: Pioneer CDJ-100S
pages.blurb: Slot-loading deck aimed at bedroom DJs, with three jog-wheel effects (Jet, Zip, Wah); sold for about ten years.

pages.name: Pioneer CDJ-400
pages.blurb: Compact deck announced in November 2007; by Pioneer's account the first CDJ to play MP3s from a USB stick.

pages.name: Cubase VST / Logic / Pro Tools
pages.blurb: Software — Audio inside the computer: from 1996 the whole track could live on a PC or Mac, with plug-ins instead of boxes. The hardware era ends here.

pages.name: DJ with Apple Music
pages.blurb: Apple Music streaming inside Serato, rekordbox, Engine DJ and djay from March 2025; terms limit it to non-commercial use.

pages.name: E-mu Emulator / Fairlight CMI
pages.blurb: Sampler — The first samplers, priced like houses. "Planet Rock" replayed Kraftwerk by hand but took the Fairlight's stock orchestra hit, explosion and claps.

pages.name: Final Scratch
pages.blurb: Timecode vinyl — Hawtin's DE9 and the laptop DJ.

pages.name: GLI PMX 7000 / PMX 9000
pages.blurb: GLI's fader mixers with a horizontal crossfader, known as the poor man's Bozak; the PMX 9000 became a favourite of hip-hop DJs.

pages.name: Roland Jupiter-8
pages.blurb: Polysynth — The expensive one, Duran Duran's and Frankie Goes to Hollywood's synth, sampled into house from records rather than played.

pages.name: Le Maitre smoke machines
pages.blurb: English effects maker of the Pea Souper, Cloud Nine, Mini Mist and, from 1994, the G300 smoke machine.

pages.name: Max (Max/MSP)
pages.blurb: Visual patching environment begun by Miller Puckette at IRCAM, sold by Opcode from 1989–90, audio added as MSP in 1997.

pages.name: Moog modular
pages.blurb: Modular synth — Robert Moog's, heard on Switched-On Bach (1968) and I Feel Love (1977).

pages.name: NoiseTracker and ProTracker
pages.blurb: Scene rewrites of Soundtracker that became the Amiga standard for hardcore, jungle and gabber producers.

pages.name: Ortofon Concorde
pages.blurb: One-piece cartridge and headshell launched for hi-fi in 1979; the reinforced Concorde Pro of 1984 took it into club booths.

pages.name: The pirate FM rig
pages.blurb: A £250 transmitter in a box on a tower-block roof, an aerial, and infra-red, microwave and UHF links back to a hidden studio.

pages.name: Rane MP 24
pages.blurb: Rane's first DJ mixer, a crossfader desk begun at Richard Long's request, shipped from September 1986 and made until July 2006.

pages.name: reFX Nexus and Vanguard
pages.blurb: Preset-led synths for dance producers; Vanguard (2004) was programmed by Markus Krause of Tone2, with presets by Manuel Schleis.

pages.name: The Rosie (Alex Rosner's mixer)
pages.blurb: Red one-off stereo mixer with level controls and a headphone cue that Alex Rosner built for Francis Grasso at the Haven.

pages.name: Roland SH-101
pages.blurb: Monosynth — Arpeggiator and sequencer in a body that could be slung round the neck; a cheap bassline machine for hardcore and techno once the 303 got expensive.

pages.name: Splice
pages.blurb: Sample subscription service founded by Steve Martocci and Matt Aimonetti; Splice Sounds launched in 2015.

pages.name: Boiler Room and the stream
pages.blurb: Format — Boiler Room's webcam livestream (London, 2010) made the filmed DJ set a release in itself: Dekmantel's stages, Sherelle's 2019 set, HÖR's hard techno.

pages.name: Roland TB-303
pages.blurb: Bass synth — An accompaniment box that failed, then squealed: acid in Chicago (1987), London (1988) and the free parties (1993–).

pages.name: Technics SP-10 / SL-1100
pages.blurb: The direct-drive motor unit and the $330 integrated deck that came before the SL-1200; Kool Herc's own decks were SL-1100As.

pages.name: Roland TR-8 / TR-8S
pages.blurb: Drum machine — Roland's 2014 Aira TR-8 modelled the 808 and 909 circuits digitally for £399; the TR-8S (2018) added samples, the Boutique TR-08 shrank it.

pages.name: Native Instruments Traktor Scratch
pages.blurb: Native Instruments' own timecode system with the Audio 8 DJ, announced January 2007 at $669; the subject of N2IT's June 2007 claim, which ended with a licence in April 2008.

pages.name: UREI 1620
pages.blurb: UREI's integrated-circuit successor to the Bozak, with six inputs on plug-in cards; the Paradise Garage's mixer by the mid-1980s.

pages.name: Web Audio and the browser
pages.blurb: Software — The W3C's browser audio standard (drafted 2011, Recommendation 2021). This book's engine builds every kick, 303 and hoover with it in your browser.

pages.name: Beyond the Dance Floor (Rebekah Farrugia)
pages.blurb: Ethnography of DJs and producers on the American West Coast, including the Sister SF network of 1997 to 2008.

pages.name: Club Cultures and Female Subjectivity (Maria Pini)
pages.blurb: Maria Pini's book, built on women ravers' own accounts, arguing that dance culture gave women more than critics allowed.

pages.name: Boiler Room (broadcast)
pages.blurb: A webcam in a London room in 2010 that became the dance world's television.

pages.name: FACT
pages.blurb: The free magazine turned website, and the FACT mix series.

pages.name: Knowledge
pages.blurb: Drum & bass's own magazine, from Colin Steven's Brixton bedroom to the newsstand.

pages.name: Resident Advisor
pages.blurb: Started in Sydney in 2001, the website that replaced the magazines: listings, reviews, the RA podcast and the ticketing business.

pages.name: Cyberdog
pages.blurb: Camden clubwear business begun by Terry Davy and Spiros Vlahos as a market stall playing psychedelic trance.

pages.name: Bandcamp
pages.blurb: Direct-sale platform founded in 2008; bought by Epic Games in March 2022 and sold to Songtradr in October 2023.

pages.name: Cisco
pages.blurb: Shibuya importer with separate techno and house shops in Udagawacho; the slope outside is still called Cisco-zaka.

pages.name: De Underground Records
pages.blurb: Forest Gate: the Aymer brothers' shop (Uncle 22 and Randall), hardcore and jungle's east London counter.

pages.name: Dub Vendor
pages.blurb: Reggae specialist that grew from a Clapham Junction market stall to shops on Lavender Hill and Ladbroke Grove, home of the Fashion Records label.

pages.name: Gramaphone Records
pages.blurb: Chicago's dance shop on North Clark Street: Derrick Carter and Mark Farina behind the counter.

pages.name: Idle Hands
pages.blurb: Bristol's shop and label on City Road, by Stokes Croft; dubstep's and techno's counter in the 2010s.

pages.name: Lighthouse Records
pages.blurb: Deep house, techno and disco shop opened in Shibuya in 2008, by 2025 in a basement in Kanda-Surugadai.

pages.name: Manhattan Records
pages.blurb: Founded behind Shibuya police station in 1980; its move to Udagawacho in 1992 or 1993 drew the import shops that made the district.

pages.name: Pure Groove
pages.blurb: The UK garage counter where the two-step white labels went first, from a Camden stall in 1988 to Holloway Road and then Smithfield.

pages.name: Rock and Soul
queries: "Rock and Soul" New York record shop
pages.blurb: Midtown record and DJ-equipment shop opened by Shirley and Joseph Bechor in 1975 at 462 Seventh Avenue; now on West 37th Street.

pages.name: Rush Hour
pages.blurb: Amsterdam's shop, label and distributor; the Dutch techno and house counter since 1997.

pages.name: Spin Inn
pages.blurb: Manchester's import shop on Cross Street, which supplied the Chicago and New York records Mike Pickering played at the Haçienda.

pages.name: Underground Solu'shn
pages.blurb: Dance shop at 9 Cockburn Street, Edinburgh, started by three DJs and still selling twelve-inches and DJ equipment in 2026.

pages.name: Vinyl Mania
pages.blurb: Carmine Street: Larry Levan's record shop, where Garage records went on sale the Monday after he played them.

pages.name: Alan Fierstein and Acoustilog
pages.blurb: Acoustician who tuned the Paradise Garage with Richard Long and designed its four-way crossover to Acoustilog's specification.

pages.name: Capital Sound
pages.blurb: Hire company that flew 76 Martin Audio F2 cabinets and 54 Amcron amplifiers for Fantazia's Big Bang in 1993.

pages.name: Desert Storm Sound System
pages.blurb: Glasgow free party rig born in after-hours parties during the 1991 Gulf War; it took techno to Tuzla and Sarajevo with aid convoys in 1994–96.

pages.name: Duke Vin the Tickler's
pages.blurb: Vincent Forbes's Ladbroke Grove sound, built in 1955 around a £4 amplifier; by BBC News's 2009 report, thought to be the first sound system at Notting Hill Carnival.

pages.name: Kirsch Audio
pages.blurb: Felix Kirsch's loudspeaker firm in Neukölln, Berlin, known for sound reinforcement and studio monitors.

pages.name: Metro (Percival Miller)
pages.blurb: Valve-amplifier builder for Jah Shaka, Jah Tubby's and others, working from north London on 807 and KT88 valves.

pages.name: Saxon Studio International
pages.blurb: Lewisham sound of Musclehead Francis and Denis Rowe; Papa Levi, Tippa Irie, Smiley Culture and fast chat, spread on cassette.

pages.name: The Spiral Tribe rig
pages.blurb: Spiral Tribe's sound system, bought in 1991: one of the Castlemorton rigs, impounded by police in 1992, then taken to Paris and Berlin as the teknival began.

pages.name: Valve Sound System
pages.blurb: Dillinja and Lemon D's drum and bass rig, a '96K' system that needed three trucks on tour.

pages.name: Dance FM
pages.blurb: Walthamstow's house and rave pirate of 1989–91 on 93.0 FM, set up by Mike Stone to sound like a legal station.

pages.name: Essential Mix
pages.blurb: BBC Radio 1's weekly two-hour guest mix, devised by producer Eddie Gordon and presented by Pete Tong since the first show on 30 October 1993.

pages.name: Pulse FM
pages.blurb: A hardcore pirate of early-1990s London on 90.6 FM, one of the rave-era stations that followed the acid house pirates.

pages.name: Unity FM
pages.blurb: A hardcore and jungle pirate of 1990s London about which almost nothing reliable has been published.
